subject: Nexa Fabric — private GPU runway and burst commitment

Subject: Nexa Fabric — private GPU runway and burst commitment

Hi Alex / Nexa infra team,

Thanks again for the call yesterday. As discussed, we're trying to lock the capacity and burst commitment language for your private deployment so we can finalize provisioning and the reserved capacity pricing. Attached is a first-pass "capacity_sizing_table.xlsx" with two scenarios:

- Steady-state: baseline QPS and 95th percentile latency targets (Sustained throughput).
- Burst runway: 15-minute to 1-hour burst envelope and acceptable tail-latency during absorption.

High-level asks from our side to validate the numbers:
1) Confirm expected QPS distribution by hour (P50/P95/P99) for the next 12 months.
2) Provide egress constraints (egress caps per region or link saturation windows).
3) Any regulatory constraints on on-prem maintenance windows that would block autoscaling/provisioning (we need warm-pool behavior).

We included initial suggested commitments: 1.2k sustained concurrent tokens/sec (combined) with a 3x burst multiplier for 20 minutes and a warm-pool of 10% of peak. Those are placeholders — please replace with your observed load where available.

Next steps: if you can return a completed sizing table and confirm acceptance of our proposed warm-pool and admission-control windows by EOD Wednesday (Aug 18), we can produce a final MOU and the DocuSign link for procurement.

Thanks — looking forward to landing this.

—Grace
Grace O'Connor

Grace — thanks for the clear template. Quick answers from our side and a couple of clarifying asks: 

1) Baseline traffic: current production profile (last 30 days): average sustained QPS 420 (P50 token/sec equivalent ~ 460), P95 ~ 1.1k, P99 spikes up to 2.8k for short windows. We can export per-hour histograms if helpful.
2) Egress: Our on-prem egress to your control plane is capped at 6Gbps per site during peak business hours; we can provision a burst lane to 12Gbps for emergency windows but that requires 48 hours notice to our network ops.
3) Maintenance windows: weekly patch window Saturdays 01:00-04:00 UTC where we cannot accept rolling reboots that impact stateful GPU pods (we can do cold replenishment). Warm-pool maintenance must avoid that window.

Concerns: the proposed 3x burst multiplier sounds fine but our testing indicates we need to pin a fast-fail fallback (quantized model variant) after 8 minutes of sustained absorption to keep tail latency under control. Can you provide the expected degradation profile if fallback model is used (token throughput delta and latency delta)? Also – how does Redwood handle KV-cache priming during burst?

We'll fill your spreadsheet and return by tomorrow morning with the hourly histogram attached.

Best,
Alex Torres
Head of Infrastructure, Nexa Fabric

Alex / Grace — quick technical reply with concrete numbers so procurement has something to sign off on. I've attached a short CSV with our runway calculations (runway_calcs.csv). Highlights:

- Fallback model: quantized v1.3 reduces token throughput per GPU by ~2.8x but reduces per-token latency by ~1.6x in high contention. In practice that means if your sustained P95 is 1.1k QPS on full model, the fallback keeps effective served requests at ~390 QPS while holding tail latency < 600ms for 95% of tokens.
- KV cache priming: we estimate warm-pool priming cost at ~12–18% extra tokens served during the first 10 minutes of a warm ramp for typical prompt reuse (prefix reuse). We recommend a staggered warmup (10% of pool every 90s) to avoid egress spikes.
- Admission control: propose a circuit-breaker at 2.6k active reqs for the node group (global per-site threshold) that moves matching requests to the quantized fallback after an 8-minute continuous exceed window. This gives a deterministic path for graceful degradation.
- Autoscale behavior: prefer proactive warm-pool (10% of peak) with elastic add-on in 5-minute increments and a max cold-start of 6 minutes for queued provision — we place the warm-pool on dedicated pre-warmed instances to meet the SLA.

Operational constraints: given your 6Gbps egress cap, assume max concurrent token encode/egress is ~1.4k sustained; crossing that requires the burst lane to 12Gbps. We can model an admission-policy that enforces egress-aware dispatch (we throttle by token weight per request).

If those degradation numbers work for you, we can bake them into the MOU and the SLA appendix. 

—Jonas

Alex — thanks for the histogram, and thanks team for the quick turn. We're in a state where procurement needs a single-page commitment summary + technical appendix to move this into SOW and DocuSign. Below is the concise commitment language we propose to include in the MOU (happy to iterate):

Proposed commitment (draft):
- Sustained throughput: Redwood will provision a private GPU pool sized to support 1.2k sustained concurrent token/sec with 95th percentile tail latency <= 450ms on the full model under normal operations.
- Burst runway: Redwood will support a 3x burst multiplier (nominal peak to 3.6k token/sec) for up to 20 minutes with automatic admission control to fallback models as necessary. Burst beyond 20 minutes subject to review and manual escalation.
- Warm-pool: 10% of peak capacity reserved as pre-warmed instances; staggered warmup to limit egress.
- Fallback policy: after 8 continuous minutes above the node-group threshold (2.6k active reqs), requests are shifted to a Redwood-verified quantized model to preserve availability; expected throughput reduction ~2.8x and tail latency target < 600ms.
- Network constraints: client must provide 48 hours notice to enable temporary burst lane to 12Gbps; otherwise admission control will enforce egress-based throttles.

Next steps: we will (1) drop this text into the MOU appendix, (2) attach the runway_calcs.csv and the filled capacity_sizing_table you return, and (3) open a DocuSign envelope for signatures. Grace — if this looks good, I'll generate the DocuSign link and CC procurement. Alex — please confirm the 48-hour notice requirement and whether the quantized fallback acceptance is okay for Helio-style inference (we'll mark that as optional in the SLA if needed).

Thanks — Karthik
